description.narrative: Projektet "Connect for Culture Africa" är ett femårigt initiativ som syftar till att öka kultursektorns roll i Afrika. Initiativet mottar finansiellt stöd från den regionala sektionen på ambassaden i Addis Abeba. Under Selams ledning ska ett nätverk av kulturförespråkare verka för att öka beslutsfattares förståelse om fördelarna med investera i kultur. Syftet är att stärka till kulturaktörers möjligheter att påverka och delta i afrikanska länders budgetprocesser. Det övergripande målet är att öka den politiska viljan kring kultursatsningar och att i slutändan se ett ökat budgetanslag till kultur och kreativa sektorer i Afrika. Initiativet ska vidare skapa förutsättningar för kultur att främja mänskliga rättigheter, demokrati, jobbskapande, teknik och digitalisering på kontinenten. Initiativet är regionalt i sin ansats med ett initialt landfokus på de fem kärnländer. Projektet kommer att utföras i nära dialog och samarbete med Afrikanska Unionen.

The "Connect for Culture Africa" project is a five-year initiative that aims to increase the role of the cultural sector in Africa. The initiative receives financial support from the regional section at the Embassy in Addis Ababa. Under Selam's leadership, a network of cultural actors will work to increase decision-makers' understanding of the benefits of investing in culture. The aim is to strengthen the opportunities for cultural actors to influence and participate in African countries' budget processes. The overall goal is to increase the political will around cultural investments and to ultimately see an increased budget allocation to culture and creative sectors in Africa. The initiative will further create the conditions for culture to promote human rights, democracy, job creation, technology and digitization on the continent. The initiative is regional in its approach with an initial country focus on the five core countries. The project will be carried out in close dialogue and collaboration with the African Union.

The project "Connect for Culture Africa" is a five-year program that aims to intertwine advocacy efforts at regional and national levels through a network of culture advocates dedicated to raising awareness on the benefits of investing in culture. The objective of the project is to contribute to increased voice among culture actors to influence and participate in budget processes that aim at securing resources to the culture and creative sectors. The project aims at contributing to an increased political will that translates to budget proposals, budget bills, and in increased budget allocation to the culture and creative sectors in Africa. The project focuses on creating conditions for culture to play its potential role in promoting human rights, democracy, job creation, tech and digitisation as well as peace and reconciliation in Africa, with an initial focus on the five core countries Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa and Morocco.

Here are the summary of results reported from 2024:
Outcome 1: Outcome 1. A consolidated, inclusive, and rights-based driven network by representatives from culture and creative sectors, as well as other key stakeholders, across the continent is advocating for the need of investing in culture, targeting the 1% budgetary commitment.
In 2024, CfCA reports that it has strengthened its regional and national networks to advocate for increased public investment in culture. National Working Groups (NWGs) were established in five countries, facilitating structured advocacy and collaboration among stakeholders. Regional meetings and participation in high-level forums supported cross-country learning and policy engagement. The network demonstrated inclusivity, with balanced gender and youth representation, and expanded its reach through digital platforms and strategic partnerships.
CfCA also enhanced members capacity for evidence-based advocacy through baseline studies and targeted workshops, contributing to policy dialogues and budget processes. Engagement with AU institutions and other regional actors is positioning CfCA as a key voice in cultural policy reform. Integration between Selam other activities such as Jazz Festival and PANAF has strengthened CfCA advocacy reach. Despite some challenges, such as inconsistent participation in certain countries, internal communication improvements helped maintain momentum. Overall, CfCA made solid progress in building a coordinated and capable advocacy network across Africa.
Outcome 2. The network is engaged in an inclusive, age and gender representative, and constructive policy dialogue with regional and national duty bearers in at least five countries targeting national budget processes and culture policies. Key stakeholders across the continent are advocating for the need of investing in culture, targeting the 1% budgetary commitment.
CfCA reports to have strengthened its advocacy through strategic partnerships and inclusive engagement. Key collaborations included formal agreements with the Ministry of Youth, Sport, and Art in Zambia, Uganda Parliamentary Forum for Creative Industries (UGAPAFOCI) and Uganda National Cultural Center (UNCC) in Uganda, and technical support from UNESCOs regional offices. These relationships enabled CfCA to influence national planning and policy processes.
The network maintained diverse representation, with 58% male and 42% female members, and 13% youth participation in National Working Groups. CfCA engaged 450 women (39%) and 485 youth (42%) across its activities, supported by standardized tools for tracking diversity. These efforts contributed to more inclusive and evidence-based policy dialogue, reinforcing CfCAs role in promoting public investment in culture across its focus countries.
Outcome 3: Young women and men culture actors have successfully participated in regional and national creative residency programs enabling their skills development and empowerment and contributing to showcases used in national and regional advocacy campaigns
CfCA reports to have empowered young cultural actors through regional and national programs that enhanced their creative, advocacy, and entrepreneurial skills. Key initiatives included the Cartoonist Residency in Ethiopia (15 artists from 5 countries), cultural policy training in Zimbabwe (60 youth, with knowledge rising from 9% to 85%), and an entrepreneurship workshop in Zambia (18 participants). The CfCA Podcast in Uganda, led by two young women, further amplified youth voices.
CfCA also integrated youth contributions into advocacy campaigns. Artworks from the residency were showcased at events like the Addis Jazz Festival, gaining wide media coverage and sparking public dialogue. Young creatives contributed to CfCAs branding and participated in advocacy tours, positioning them as active stakeholders in promoting investment in the cultural and creative industries.
Outcome 4. Demonstrated increased awareness among duty-bearers in targeted countries and the general public on the importance to invest in inclusive culture and creative industries.
CfCA reports to contributed to increased awareness among duty-bearers and the public about the importance of investing in inclusive cultural and creative industries. Through the engagement of National Working Groups, baseline studies, and collaboration with festivals and media platforms, CfCA expanded public discourse on cultural investment. A total of 442 media pieces (including 34 articles and 8 videos) were disseminated via 28 media outlets across five countries, supported by 8 articles published on CfCAs website.
Government recognition also grew. Ministries in Zambia, Zimbabwe, Ethiopia, and Uganda formally received CfCAs baseline reports, with some integrating findings into budget discussions. In Ethiopia, the Ministry of Culture used CfCAs research during its budget defense, and in Mozambique, a presidential candidate publicly endorsed the 1% funding goal for culture. These developments reflect growing political and public acknowledgment of cultures role in development, democratic values, and social cohesion.
Successes were driven by strong government engagement, formal partnerships (e.g., MoUs), and strategic media and event collaborations that amplified advocacy messages. Artist-led advocacy and committed local partners also played a key role, while peer learning through network meetings helped sustain momentum and refine strategies.
Challenges reported include some implementing partners showing capacity gaps in meeting donor requirements, prompting CfCA to expand training and technical support. Engagement with National Working Groups was inconsistent, so flexible scheduling and virtual tools were introduced to improve participation. Also, delays in staffing and baseline studies affected timelines.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
